client: I've been really struggling since starting college last semester. The workload feels impossible to keep up with, and now I've started avoiding my friends because I'm either too busy studying or too embarrassed to admit how behind I am. I'm not sure talking about it will help when what I really need is more hours in the day.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load between the academic pressure and the isolation from friends. I notice you mention feeling embarrassed—could you tell me more about what thoughts come up when you consider reaching out to your friends?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I just keep thinking they'll judge me for not having my life together. Like, everyone else seems to be doing fine with their studies and social lives, but I'm barely keeping my head above water. The idea of reaching out makes me feel pathetic, like I'm admitting I can't handle things on my own.
therapist: Your voice sounds really strained when you talk about this—it seems the fear of judgment cuts particularly deep. Would you say this belief that others have it all together holds up when you really examine how people present themselves versus how they might actually feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess I know logically that people probably don’t have it all together, but it still *feels* true when I’m in the moment. Like at work, everyone seems so confident in meetings while I’m overanalyzing every word I say. Maybe they’re just better at faking it? That doesn’t really make me feel better though.  

And honestly, even if they’re struggling too, why does that matter? It still feels like I’m the only one who can’t handle it. Like there’s something fundamentally wrong with how I react to things.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between knowing something intellectually and feeling something very different emotionally—that must be exhausting. When you say "fundamentally wrong," what specifically do you imagine might be broken or lacking in how you handle challenges?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I don't know, it's like my brain just freezes up whenever something stressful happens. I can logically understand that I'm probably overreacting, but in the moment it feels like I'm fundamentally broken because I can't handle normal challenges like other people seem to. 

The worst part is I'll beat myself up afterwards for not handling things better, which just makes me more anxious about the next challenge. It's this exhausting cycle.
therapist: Your voice drops when you describe this cycle—it sounds like you're carrying both the initial stress and then a second layer of self-criticism about how you handled it. What do you think would happen if, just once, you met that moment of freezing up with curiosity instead of criticism?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know if I could actually do that. When I freeze up, it feels like my brain just stops working, and then afterwards all I can think is how stupid I must have looked. Trying to be curious in that moment seems... impossible. It's like asking me to suddenly speak another language when I'm already panicking.
therapist: It sounds like that moment of freezing feels completely overwhelming, like you're trapped in it. When you describe this, I hear both frustration and a deep desire to handle things differently—that tells me you haven't given up on yourself, even if it feels impossible right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it does feel overwhelming, like I’m stuck in a loop I can’t break out of. I want to handle things differently, but every time I try, it’s like my brain just shuts down, and I end up feeling worse for not being able to push through. I guess I haven’t given up on myself, but it’s hard to see how I’ll ever get past this.
therapist: I hear how exhausting this loop feels—like you're running into the same wall every time you try to push through. That moment when your brain shuts down sounds particularly frightening. Could we slow down and explore what happens right before that shutdown begins?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
It's like this heavy fog rolls in right before my brain shuts down. I'll be trying to focus on work or a conversation, and suddenly everything feels too loud and bright, like my thoughts are scrambling to run away. The worst part is knowing it's coming but feeling powerless to stop it - that's when the panic really starts building.  

I've tried deep breathing and all that, but in the moment it just feels...insulting? Like putting a bandaid on a broken bone. Do you really think slowing down helps when my brain's already racing?
therapist: Your description of the fog rolling in is so vivid—it sounds like you're acutely aware of the shift happening in your mind and body. When you say deep breathing feels "insulting," I wonder if that's because it doesn't match the intensity of what you're experiencing in those moments. Could we explore what might feel more grounding to you when that fog starts to settle?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, deep breathing just feels... too small, you know? Like trying to stop a tidal wave with a teaspoon. When the fog comes, it's like my whole body tenses up and my thoughts start racing. Maybe something more physical would help, but I don't know what wouldn't feel silly or forced.
therapist: It makes sense that deep breathing might feel too small when you're describing something as overwhelming as a tidal wave. The way you describe your whole body tensing up suggests this is a full-body experience. What comes to mind when you think about physical actions that might match the intensity of what you're feeling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, I guess deep breathing does feel too... small, like you said. When the anxiety hits, it's like my whole body's bracing for impact. I've tried squeezing stress balls before, but it just makes me more aware of how tense I am. 

Honestly, sometimes I feel like I need to just... run or punch something, but that's not exactly practical when I'm at work or on the subway. And then I feel stupid for even thinking that way.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it is to feel like your body needs big movement when you're in spaces where that's not possible. That urge to run or punch sounds like your body's natural way of trying to release the tension—it's not stupid at all. What do you think would happen if you tried channeling that energy into something more subtle, like pressing your palms together really firmly or stretching your legs under the desk?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess pressing my palms together could help a little, but it feels like putting a bandaid on a broken bone. When the anxiety hits that hard, I need to move my whole body or I feel like I'll explode. Even thinking about trying to contain it makes my chest feel tighter. 

I'm worried those small movements will just make me more aware of how much I can't actually move freely. Like I'll be hyper-focused on restraining myself instead of releasing anything. Does that make sense?
therapist: It makes complete sense—when your body is screaming for big movement, small adjustments might feel like another form of restraint rather than relief. That fear of hyper-focusing on containment instead of release is really understandable. What if we explored ways you could honor that need for full-body movement in small bursts, even in public spaces? Like finding a bathroom stall to stretch in or taking the stairs when possible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
